   since WP 6.2 slice 6. Recorded here so a later session does not read Phase
   5's exit list as a claim that it went green.
2. **The four unused `@ts-expect-error` directives are in gate suites**, and
   deleting them is a change to four files whose job is to be trustworthy, for
   no behavioural reason. They are baselined with that stated rather than
   quietly swept.

### WP 5.2b — Input tables: the section SuReSuite has never had · 2026-09-18 · no migration

**What the previous entry promised.** D57's gap check named two things and
neither changed this package: that `npm run lint` cannot pass, and that four
`@ts-expect-error` directives are baselined on purpose. Both held.

**Twelve pages, twelve of twelve.** Eleven table references plus "Units and time
periods". Section 3 is complete and `registry.test.ts` knows it: the count
assertion is now a table of finished sections with the package that finished
each, so "section 3 is done" is something the suite asserts rather than
something a §16 entry claims.

**── THE INSTRUCTION THIS PACKAGE WAS GIVEN WAS STALE, AND THE CORRECTION IS
ITS OPPOSITE ──**

§12 and §17 both said 5.2b must **reassign four pages** to packages that could
ship them: `node_list`, `network_nodes`, `network_edges` (deferred to WP 4.2)
and `multi_tier_supply_chain` (WP 3.1), on the grounds that none had a sidecar
and none could therefore be generated.

All four have sidecars. `multi_tier_supply_chain` was described in WP 3.2 rather
than deferred a third time (D58's own row says so), and WP 4.3 described the
other three at tier 3 — which is how D54's largest deferral group closed. The
instruction was written in WP 5.2a, before Phase 3 and Phase 4 ran, and nothing
between then and now would have said it had expired. **This is R8's shape on a
sentence rather than on a defect**: an instruction pointing at work that has
already been done reads exactly like an instruction pointing at work that has
not. Both rows are corrected, and the correction is recorded rather than the
sentence deleted, because the interesting thing is that it was stale rather than
that it is now right.

**── THE FINDING: A DATA FACT AUTHORED TWICE, FOUND BY NEEDING A THIRD (D101) ──**

`network_nodes` and `node_list` each hold columns a person uploaded beside
columns an analysis wrote, which is why "what tier is this table" had no answer
for three packages. A page in section 3 has to tell the reader which half is
theirs. There were exactly two places that knew:

1. prose in each column's sidecar `meaning` and `note` — "ANALYSIS OUTPUT — …";
2. a literal `COMPUTED_COLUMNS` Set of eighteen names inside
   `graphHashCoverage.test.ts`, which is the rule WP 5.3 replaced the
   four-table exclusion list with and the thing every "no analysis output is
   inside the hash" assertion turns on.

Neither is readable by a generator, and a page typing a third list is D21
exactly. So the fact is **declared**: `computed_by` on the sidecar column
schema, naming the analyzer that writes it. The generator emits it, the pages
render the split from it, and **`graphHashCoverage.test.ts` derives its Set from
the contract instead of holding one** — 18 of 18, byte-identical to the literal
it replaced, verified before the swap rather than after. The suite also asserts
the derived set is non-empty before the loop that uses it, because a contract
declaring none would make that loop examine nothing and pass, which is the
vacuity D57 was.

That is one authoring where there were two, and it closes on the side that
matters: the next analyzer column declares itself in the sidecar the migration's
author is already editing, rather than in a test file they have no reason to
open.

**── THE RULE THAT SHAPED EVERY PAGE, AND THE ONE COLUMN THAT DEFEATED IT ──**

§6.3 section 3 gives every uploaded column an "If you leave it blank" line, and
T1 says it resolves to data, a named rule or an explicit default — there is no
fourth option. `blankBehaviour()` resolves it from the contract through four
ordered sources and **returns which one answered**, so the page labels it:
`required` · `substituted` · `engine default` · `passed through`. When none
answers it returns `unknown` and the page prints a blind-spot line. There is no
branch that writes a plausible sentence.

Measured across the whole contract, **nine uploaded columns have no sourceable
blank behaviour and eight of them are `tier2_suppliers`/`tier3_suppliers`'s**.
The ninth, `bom_multi_level.higher_level_component_id`, is answered by the
engine's `transform` ("NULL means 'the product'") rather than by a
`missing_default` — which is why the fourth source exists at all, and it is the
weakest of the four on purpose: it describes behaviour rather than declaring a
rule, so it is consulted last and labelled differently.

**Which is how D102 was found.** Those two tables are described, are offered by
the upload wizard with templates and required headers, and **have no page in the
manual**: §6.3 section 3 enumerates eleven and neither is among them. A user
holding `tier2_suppliers.csv` has a working upload and no page explaining one
column of it — and it is also the pair with the most unexplained columns in the
contract. Not fixed here: adding two pages changes the site map, and WP 5.2's
own exit gap check ("diff the §6.3 inventory against the live schema and
`App.tsx`") is scoped to make exactly that call.

**── A SECOND GATE, BECAUSE THE FIRST ONE NEVER EXECUTED A PAGE ──**

`registry.test.ts` asserts the site map's SHAPE. Nothing in it renders anything,
so a page that reads a field the generator stopped emitting passes every
assertion and is a blank screen. `bodies.test.tsx` renders every live body to
static markup and requires real output, the registry's own title in the `h1`,
and no raw markdown code span.

**It found three pages printing backticks on its first run, all of them WP
5.2a's and 5.2h's.** `AllTables` and `FieldIndex` rendered `c.unit` raw, and
`unit` is a contract string written in code spans ("units per `time_unit`");
`AllTables` and `DataModelAtAGlance` rendered the undescribed group's `why` raw.
Forty-six visible backticks on the reference page alone, since WP 5.2h emitted
it. `Prose` existed the whole time and was already used two lines away — which
is the point: this is not a mistake anybody would make while looking, and
nothing was looking. One of this package's own components had it too, caught the
same way.

**── THE PACKAGE'S ONE IDEA: THE MANUAL AND THE GATE ARE THE SAME DERIVATION ──**

WP 6.1 derived every grid field's chain — 38 of them, eleven broken, each claim
carrying a `file:line` — and pinned the eleven as a ratchet in
`resolutionChains.test.ts`. §6.3 section 5 has to show that to a user, and there
were three ways to do it: write the chains down (D21, and WP 6.1's own opening
sentence is that ~120 hand-written chains are true on the day they are typed),
derive them a second time in the browser (two implementations of one fact), or
run the real one.

`scripts/data-contract/chains.mjs` runs the real one. esbuild bundles
`resolutionChains.ts` to CommonJS so `generate.mjs` can `require()` it without
becoming async, and it is called with **exactly** the sources
`resolutionChains.test.ts` passes — which is not tidiness: §4 D91 is what
happened when that source list held `project_map.py` alone, and a manual reading
a narrower tree than the gate would publish a different answer from the one CI
enforces. The result lands in `src/components/docs/generated/policy.generated.ts`
through `renderAll`, so it is covered by the drift comparison that already runs
on every pull request. Proved by editing `BROKEN_COUNT` in the committed
artifact: `contract:generate -- --check` goes red.

**What the pages then say.** Each stage page renders its columns from
`STAGE_TABLE_SPEC` — the grid's own object, imported, not copied — and marks
every broken chain **as prominently as the column it belongs to**, with one
headline per shape:

| shape | what the page tells the reader |
|---|---|
| `overridden` | "The engine works this out itself and ignores what you type" |
| `legacy-only` | "Editing this changes nothing in the strategic engine" |
| `app-routing` | "This steers the app, not the simulation" |
| `unread` | "Nothing reads this value at all" |
| `no-target` | "There is nowhere for this value to be stored" |

`reorder_point` is the one worth the paragraph it gets: the grid accepts a
number, stores it, versions it and hashes it into the policy fingerprint, and
both engines compute the reorder point for themselves. A page that listed the
column and stopped would be describing a screen.

**── THE FINDING: THE TRUST REPORT PUBLISHES TWO LIMITS THAT ARE NO LONGER TRUE
(D103) ──**

`knownLimits()` in `src/lib/trust/trustReport.ts` appends two entries
unconditionally, and both are stale:

1. *"The dataset hash does not cover the deep-tier network"*, citing D75 —
   **which WP 5.3 closed**. `20260917000009` folded exactly those six columns
   into `hash_network` at `schema_version` 3.
2. *"Sixteen database functions write data without naming the person who ran
   them"* — **which WP 6.2 slices 11 and 12 closed**. Twelve took the actor
   parameter in `20260918000002`–`20260918000003`; the four remaining are not
   debt, and `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` now fails if a name sits on that list
   without one of two justifications.

Both go to users, on every project, in the artifact whose entire purpose is to
be the honest one. And the block's own docstring names the trap it fell into —
*"A limits block that is identical for every project is a disclaimer; one that
changes with the data is a finding"* — because the two entries ABOVE these are
recomputed per project every time and these two are recomputed never. It is D21
one layer in: a prose fact about the data layer, authored inside a code module,
with nothing comparing it to §4.

**Not fixed here, and the reason is not only scope.** The module is WP 4.4's and
the second entry's correct figure is WP 6.2's to state. What Phase 5 could do
was stop republishing them, and it does: `data-trust-report` documents the
report's sections and its three freshness states and repeats neither sentence.

**Three freshness states, and the page says so in its own callout.**
`fresh` · `stale` · **`unknown` — we cannot tell.** Rendering `unknown` as
`stale` answers a question with a guess and rendering it as `fresh` is worse;
the third state exists so the report can decline, which is the only honest thing
it can do about a row written before anything recorded where it came from.

**Two smaller corrections.** §6.3 said "The policy catalog — **all 21**"; the
registry declares **23**, and the page renders the count rather than carrying
one, so the section map now says "every policy the registry declares" instead of
a number that was already wrong. And three of this package's pages document a
table the contract does not describe — `policy_versions`, `policy_presets`
(WP 6.4) and `model_validations` (WP 6.3). Each page says which package owes the
column reference, reading the owner from the coverage register rather than
naming it, and none of the three writes a column list by hand.

**The bundle baseline was re-recorded, and the direction matters.**
`total-js` 1699.6 → **1799.3 kB**; `initial-graph` 194.3 → **159.4 kB**. Every
byte of the growth is in the lazy `DocPage` chunk (111.9 kB gzip), which a
reader fetches only on `/docs`; the initial graph did not move at all and the
re-record RATCHETS ITS CEILING DOWN by 35 kB, because the old number had been
loose since before the route splitting. The baseline's own note says never
re-record to admit a regression, and this is not one — but it will be crossed
again by 5.2d–g, and a session that re-records without measuring which chunk
grew is doing the thing the note forbids.

   2→3 boundary review invented after seven defects were carried that way, and
   it fired here on its own, three phases later, against a row written by
   somebody who had read it.
2. **Nothing gates a prose fact inside `src/`.** `check:docs` enforces
   single-source across *markdown*; D103 is the same defect in TypeScript, and
   D101 was the same defect in a test file. Three instances in two packages is a
   class, not a coincidence. A rule that scanned `src/` and `supabase/` for
   sentences citing a D-number and resolved them against §4 would have caught
   all three; it is not written here because deciding what counts as a citable
   claim in code is a design question, not a Phase 5 one.
3. **`policy.generated.ts` embeds the engine's file paths in a shipped
   bundle.** Each hop carries its `file:line` evidence, and that is the point —
   a reader can check the claim. It also means `scsim/scsim/io/project_map.py`
   and `sim-worker/sim_worker/engine.py:320` are strings in the client bundle.

### WP 6.3 (slice 15) — D88 was never waiting on adoption · 2026-09-19 · no migration

**What slice 14 promised.** That D88's precondition was adoption, not code, and
needed "one analyzer run against functions deployed after 20:27". That run
happened. It did not work, and the reason corrects the row rather than
satisfying it.

**The measurement.** A metrics calculation on the `Aumovio` project, reported by
its own UI as successful, against edge functions whose workflow had reported
green at 20:27 (§15 run `35398461411`):

```
| project  | node_list | network_nodes | network_edges | nodes_with_metrics |
| Aumovio  | 439       | 439           | 0             | 439                |

analysis_runs 0 · analysis_results 0
no_provenance 9016 of 9016   (was 8577 of 8577 — the total went UP by Aumovio's 439)
```

439 rows written AFTER the dual-write shipped, every one carrying computed
columns, not one carrying `computed_from_hash`, and no run to carry it.

**D104 — twelve of eighteen edge functions never reach production from CI.**
`supabase-functions.yml` names six and nothing else. The four analyzers are not
among them. Neither is `ingest-file`, which is WP 3.2's entire deliverable and
which §2.1 `ingestion-contract` describes as a live second source.

**What hid it for two packages.** `supabase/functions/_shared/**` IS a path
trigger. A change to `analysisStore.ts` therefore fires this workflow, it handles
its six and goes green, and the run appears in the history as a success on the
very commit that shipped the dual-write. An edge function bundles its imports at
publish time, so the analyzers went on running the `_shared/` of whenever they
were last pushed by hand. Every signal said it had landed.

**This corrects D88 rather than closing it.** Its owner column reads "the
unblocking condition is a NUMBER … `analysis_results` non-zero for a project".
The number is still 0, but not for the reason given: adoption happened and the
code was never there to adopt.

**Four added here, eight deliberately not.** The analyzers are added because they
are what D88 waits on and their source is CI-green. The other eight stay off:
each has been running an unknown build for an unknown time, and pushing
`delete-project` or `erp-sync-orbit-mrp` sight-unseen is a production change
whose blast radius nobody has measured. They need diffing against production one
at a time, which is a package and not a line in a YAML file.

**The gate is unwritten and this slice does not write it.** Nothing compares the
functions the repo holds against the functions the workflow names. That check is
the real fix — the same shape as `table-covered`, where a table is either
described or deferred to a named package — and it would have caught this on the
day WP 4.3 merged. Sized, not taken.

**A second finding, unrelated to provenance and not chased here.** `Aumovio` has
439 nodes and **zero** `network_edges`. Degree, betweenness, closeness and
eigenvector centrality over an edgeless graph are degenerate, so the 439 metrics
now stored may be numbers with no meaning — T1's own subject. Whether the
analyzer should refuse an edgeless graph rather than score it belongs with D72.

### WP 5.2f — Computed tables and reproducibility: the page that cannot describe a feature · 2026-09-18 · no migration

**What the previous package promised.** 5.2e's gap check named D104 (bare
filenames in §4, three fixed and eight still exposed), the eighteen

**── THE PACKAGE'S HARD PAGE, AND IT IS HARD BECAUSE THE FEATURE IS NOT THERE ──**

`reproducibility-record` documents A5 — every result bound to its dataset,
policy set, scenario and engine version. **Two invariants behind it are not met**
and the page says so in the reader's words rather than describing a working
feature:

- **`result-binding` (I8)** — the single artifact binding all four does not
  exist; it is WP 6.3's. The page's honest sentence is that *a result is
  reproducible in pieces rather than as a record*, followed by what to do
  instead: freeze a dataset version and save a policy version BEFORE the run,
  then export all three workbooks and keep them together. Assembly by hand, and
  it works.
- **`input-hash` (I5)** — the dual-write is shipped and correct, and **every
  derived row that exists carries no stamp**, because nobody has run an analysis
  since it shipped (§4 D88: 8 577 of 8 577, with an empty store). The page says
  the columns exist on four tables, that the analyses fill them from the run
  rather than from a parameter so a row cannot name a world its run never saw,
  and then that **they cannot be back-filled** — a row written before the anchor
  existed has no hash, and inventing one is fabricated provenance, which is worse
  than an empty column because an empty column is legible as "we do not know".

Which of the four tables carry the provenance columns is read from the
contract's `computed_by` declarations rather than asserted, so a table that
gained or lost them changes the page with no edit. And the page names the one
table that deliberately has none — the deep-tier edges, every column of which is
uploaded — because a stamp no writer could fill is a promise, not a fact.

`dataset_versions.hash_network`'s sidecar said the network domain is

said all three hold zero rows so the column is "the digest of an empty domain on

`20260917000009` — WP 5.3, the migration that CLOSED D75 — folded the deep-tier
topology into that domain: the six columns the two prominence RPCs return from
`network_nodes` and `network_edges`, at `schema_version` 3. So the description
was two tables short and the note's central claim had stopped being true on the
same commit, since the deep-tier tables are not empty.

**The manual renders that sentence.** `dataset-versions` shows each hash
column's own contract description, which is the right design and is why this was
found at all: the drift was one page away from being published to users. The
migration's `COMMENT ON FUNCTION` says the right thing; the sidecar simply did
not follow it.

Corrected here, with the note recording that it was wrong and why rather than
being quietly rewritten. **That is the third instance of one class in three
packages** — D101 (a computed-column list in a test file), D103 (two stale
limits in the Trust Report), D105 (a hash description in a sidecar) — and the
class is: a prose fact about the data layer, authored outside §4, with nothing
comparing the two. `check:docs` enforces exactly this for markdown and for
nothing else.

**`supply_chain_data` gained its `computed_by` declarations.** WP 5.2b annotated

### WP 5.2g — Connectors, access and the API: the manual is complete · 2026-09-18 · no migration

**What the previous package promised.** 5.2d's gap check named D106 and D107,
the ten tables documented behaviourally, and `kpis-and-resilience-index`
reaching past the access layer. All three stand; the ten is now the subject of
this package's own exit check.

**Fourteen pages.** Section 10 (three), section 13 (seven), section 14 (four).
**80 of 80. Zero stubs. Every section of §6.3 is written.**

**── FOUR UNCOMFORTABLE THINGS, SAID IN THE READER'S WORDS ──**

`who-can-see-your-data` is the load-bearing page of this package and every
number on it is computed from the contract rather than typed, so it cannot
become optimistic by going stale.

1. **Identity is asserted, not proved.** This application authenticates against
   its own approved-user list held in the browser, so the user id arriving with
   a write is client-asserted (§4 D28). What IS real is stated beside it — the
   database refuses a landing into a project that user cannot reach, checked
   server-side — and then the limit: an audit row names the identity the client
   presented. `account-and-password` says the same thing to the person whose
   password it is, which is where they will meet it.
2. **"RLS: enabled" is not the assurance it sounds like, and there are THREE
   states.** The page counts the described tables with row-level security on,
   the ones whose every policy permits every row, and — the third state — the
   ones the static replay **cannot determine**. It then tells the story that
   makes the third state necessary: the item masters were recorded as having it
   off, and executing the migration found it *on, with rules that permit
   everything* (WP 2.4). Wrong in both directions at once, which is why
   `determinate: false` is carried into the generated module rather than
   collapsed into `false`.
3. **`min_project_role` is declared on all 48 described tables and read by ONE
   live path** (§4 D66). The page names the disagreement concretely: an editor
   who is not the project's modeler passes the promotion's role gate and is then
   refused by the row rules on the very rows they were promoting. Two gates
   asking different questions about one action, and only one of them decides.
4. **The API principal is a key, not a person.** Three calls in the public API
   write with no actor, and the page explains why a fabricated uuid would be
   worse — an audit trail reading as though somebody acted when nobody did.

**`endpoints-and-schemas` is generated from the dispatcher's own route table.**
§6.3 marks it **G**; the data contract describes tables and not an HTTP surface,
so the strongest declaration that exists is the `routes` literal the dispatcher
matches against. 19 routes, 7 scopes, parsed with a hard failure below ten. That
is D90's weakest door for the third time this phase, and the page's footer says
so — and it also says what is NOT there: request and response bodies are
declared nowhere a generator can read, so the page ships an accurate endpoint
list with no schemas rather than a complete-looking page that is wrong in six
months.

**── WP 5.2'S EXIT GAP CHECK ──**

*"Diff the §6.3 inventory against the live schema and `App.tsx`; a table or
route with no page and no internal-only justification is a finding."* Run:

**Routes.** 28 in `App.tsx`. Every project-facing one has a page. The rest are
shell (`/`, `/auth`, `/app`, `/forbidden`, `/about`, `/docs`, `/help`,
`/help/:slug`) or a connector callback, none of which a user manual has a page
for. **No finding.**

**Tables.** 81 in the schema, 48 described, **18 described tables have no
narrative page**. Thirteen are machinery §6.3 never promised a page for —
staging tables, the capability grid, the policy stores, `risk_data` — and all
eighteen are in "All tables" with every column. **Five are worth naming**:

- `analysis_runs`, `analysis_results` — the store rather than a user surface,
  and `performance-and-caching` and `network-science-metrics` describe what it
  does. Defensible.
- `tier2_suppliers`, `tier3_suppliers` — **D102**, found in 5.2b and still open:
  described, uploadable through the wizard, and absent from §6.3's eleven.
- **`customers` — D108, and this is the finding.** Tier 2, sidecar'd, its grain
  calls it "the demand-side counterpart of `suppliers`", and `suppliers` has a
  page while this has none. It has **no `ingest_dataset`**, nothing in the
  product writes it (§4 D94), and `P-C.2` reads two of its columns on every run.
  Two fields the engine consumes, on a table a user can neither upload, edit nor
  read about. The missing page is the smallest of the three problems and the one
  that makes the other two visible.

**Ten tables are documented behaviourally rather than by column**, across three
packages, because the contract does not describe them: `policy_versions`,
`policy_presets`, `model_validations`, `external_evidence`, `scenarios`,
`sim_scenarios`, `scenario_templates`, `recovery_playbooks`, `run_item_series`,
`user_files`. Every one of those pages names the work package that owes the
reference, reading the owner from the coverage register, and **not one writes a
column list by hand**. That discipline held ten times and it has a cost: a
reader on those pages gets prose where every other reference page gives them a
column, a unit and a blank-cell rule.

### WP 5.2i — The door a figure comes through · 2026-09-19 · no migration

**What the previous package promised, and what it missed.** 5.2g reported the
manual complete: 80 of 80 pages, zero stubs, every section written, every gate
green. All of that is true and it was not the whole picture, which a reader
said in one sentence — *there are a lot missing, and I have figures I cannot
use.*

Both halves check out, and the numbers are worth writing down rather than
softening.

**── THE FIGURE GAP (D109) ──**

Three figures across eighty pages. All three are WP 5.2a's inline SVGs.
**WP 5.2b–g added zero.**

It is not a lapse of taste, it is structural: there is no image component in
`prose.tsx`, no asset folder, no convention, and `Figure` takes `children` so
nothing would have failed if a page had tried. PLAN.md's own header names
**eleven diagrams** in an artifact this repository does not have; §6.5 records
the decision not to link them. Between that decision and this package, nobody
built the alternative — so a reader holding figures for their own application
had nowhere to put one, and nothing in the repository explained why.

**The door**: `src/assets/manual/` + `figureManifest.ts` + `DocFigure`. A figure
is **one file plus one line**. `import.meta.glob` resolves the folder at build
time, so there is no import to write, no path that works in dev and 404s in
production, and no generator to remember. Verified end to end by dropping a file
in and reading the emitted `<img>`, then removing it.

**Sixteen slots, declared and open.** Each names its page, the filename it
wants, and a `shows` brief saying what the diagram must contain to be right —
so an author is told what to draw rather than asked to guess. An unfilled slot
renders a labelled placeholder rather than nothing, which is §5.3 T3 applied to
the manual's own illustrations: a figure that silently fails to appear is the
one kind of broken a reader cannot report.

**The three existing SVGs became FALLBACKS, not casualties.** A slot with a file
supersedes the schematic; a slot without one falls back to it. Dropping a real
diagram onto those three pages is a replacement, and nothing regresses while the
slots are empty.

`figures.test.ts` draws the line where it belongs: an **open slot is reported,
not failed** — the manual ships with slots unfilled on purpose — while a **file
no slot uses FAILS**, because a dead asset in a repository is a file nobody can
tell is dead. It also refuses alt text that duplicates the caption: they do
different jobs, and copying one into the other is how a figure ends up
explaining nothing twice.

**── THE THIN PAGES, MEASURED ──**

Rendering every page and counting words: median 805, and **thirty pages under
450**. The distribution is the finding. The generated reference pages are
substantial — "All tables" is 23 000 words — and **the narrative pages are
thin**, which is exactly backwards: the generated half was never at risk of
being under-written, because a generator cannot be lazy.

The worst of them were the four network pages, averaging **332 words**, for
screens whose entire purpose is visual — and with no picture either. What they
omitted was not prose, it was the product: the four inferred node groups and the
fact that a mis-typed id silently becomes a fifth node; the zero-flow filter
that is on by default and hides exactly the rows worth auditing; supplier
diversity and single-source risk; revenue coverage as the figure that qualifies
every weighted measure on the firm page; the level-connectivity summary and what
a one-node level means. All of it visible in the pages themselves and none of it
in the manual.

Four rewritten here, from the page sources, to **870 words average**. Twenty-three
remain under 500 and are named in the gap check.

0 of 16 filled · `contract:check` ✓ · `typecheck` ✓ 28 of 28 held ·
`check:docs` ✓ · `build` ✓ · `audit:bundle` clean, initial graph 155.7 kB ·
eslint **336/116** and `audit:ui` **8**, at baseline.

**Gap check.** Three findings:

1. **D109 closes the door's absence and not the diagrams.** Sixteen briefs are
   written; sixteen figures are not drawn. The fill rate is printed by the test
   on every run so it cannot quietly stay at zero.
2. **Twenty-three pages are still under 500 words**, and they cluster:
   sections 9, 10, 11 and 14 — the assistant, connectors, results and the API.
   Those are the sections furthest from the data contract, which is the same
   pattern as the network pages: where there was no generated fact to render,
   less was written. That correlation is the useful finding, because it predicts
   where to look next rather than describing what happened.
3. **`registry.test.ts` counts pages and nothing counts what is on them.**
   Eighty live pages with a body is what the gate asserts; a 260-word page and a
   1 600-word page are identical to it. A floor — even a low one — would have
   caught the network pages before a reader did. Not added here, because picking
   the number is a judgement about what a short page is allowed to be, and a
   threshold set carelessly is one that gets raised until it means nothing.


### WP 8.0 — The graph layer, measured before it is changed · 2026-09-19 · no migration

**What the previous package promised.** Phase 5 closed with the manual complete
and its gap check pointing at what eighty pages had no picture of — and four of
the shortest pages in it were the four **network** pages, "averaging 332 words
with no picture, describing screens whose entire purpose is visual" (D109's own
words). That was recorded as a documentation finding. It was not one. A reader
then said the same thing from the other side: the Process- and Product-level maps
**look wrong**, and Process-level is missing what Product-level has.

**Both halves of that are true, and the second one inverts.** Process-level is the
LARGER page — 1 849 lines against 1 412 — and it has affordances Product-level
lacks: a hover-tooltip node type, an on-canvas legend, a labels toggle, a
per-depth colour ramp, loading and empty overlays, a level-connectivity table.
What it has none of is **analytics**: no centrality, no prominence, no map, no
risk, no provenance strip. The gap runs both ways, which is why WP 8.4 is a table
with two columns and not a list of things to copy in one direction.

**And the mapping really is wrong, mechanically.** Thirteen defects opened, D112
to D124. The root cause is one sentence long and it is in the contract already:
`supply_chain_data.from_location` is *"a supplier, a material, or the plant,
depending on which lane produced it"* — **there is no type column on either edge
table**, so eight independent classifiers each invent one at render time, from a
different signal, and they disagree by construction. A node that is both an
inbound source and a BOM source is `material` in SQL, either A or B on
Product-level depending on row order, `supplier` on Process-level, and **dropped
from the map entirely**.

**── WHY THIS PACKAGE MEASURES AND CHANGES NOTHING ──**

The diagnosis BRANCHES on a number this repository does not hold.
`ProcessLevelNetwork.tsx`'s ladder calls level 5 a supplier; the ETL writes the
inbound lane at `max BOM depth + 1`. So the ladder is right on a BOM exactly four
levels deep and wrong on every other depth — and the layout was last tuned
against a four-deep dataset (`1b90687`). Whether the reader's project is
D112 live or D112 latent with something else on screen is a fact about
**production**, and no work-package session can reach production.

So: **seven probes, every one a `select`, across EVERY project** rather than the
one §15 names — because D42's lesson is that the largest project in this database
is the one the seeder creates, and reading it alone reports a clean data layer
that is not clean. `bom_level` and the source counts (D115); the `level`
histogram per lane; empty endpoints (D114); nodes at more than one level (D113);
nodes in more than one lane role (D116); `node_list` against the multi-tier node
set (D117); `data_source_group` and the NULL level (D118, D119). Each one prints
per-project rows and a verdict sentence that names the defect it sizes.

**No migration in these pushes — and the standing rule about the three doors is
now WEAKER than it reads, which this package had to establish before following
it.** `supabase-migrations.yml` was scoped to `branches: [main]` on 2026-09-18,
which closes §4 D31's first half: a feature-branch push no longer deploys, so the
race that lost three §15 runs across two packages cannot happen off `main` at all.
CLAUDE.md still describes the old behaviour. **A second consequence nobody had
written down**: because `verification-sql.yml` fires on the runner's own path, a
push that changes probes IS the verify request — no `.github/verify-request` touch
is needed, and this package's two §15 runs were both triggered that way. The rule
that matters now is narrower and still worth keeping: a push carrying a migration
must not also change the runner, because a `main` merge would then order two
workflows with nothing between them.

**── D123: §16 WAS NOT §16, AND THIS PACKAGE FOUND IT BY NEEDING TO WRITE IN IT ──**

`check.mjs`'s `section16()` slices from `## 16.` to `## 17.`. The document had been
appending drift-log entries **after §17's sequencing table** since
`WP 6.2 (slice 1)`. So R7's append-only half was protecting 38 entries and could
not see 21, and R7's second half — "every done package has a §16 entry" — would
have accepted a done package whose entry landed out there.

It reads exactly like §16 to a person and not at all like §16 to the gate. That is
D101's and D105's shape arriving through a heading's POSITION instead of through a
duplicated fact, and nothing in the repository could have said so, because the
rule that reads §16 cannot report on text it does not consider part of §16.

Closed by moving §17 to the end, so §16 runs to it and §18 (Phase 8) follows in
numeric order. **No entry was added or edited**: `contract:check` now reports
**59 entries where it reported 38**, and R7's append-only half re-reads **119
revisions** of the section against the new boundary and holds.

**── WHY PHASE 8 AND NOT PHASE 7, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL ──**

The plan this package executes called it Phase 7. §14 already contains
`WP 7.1 — The authentication model`, and §4 D28 is owned by it — an owner added
deliberately at WP 3.4 *because* D28 had been owned by a finished phase and R8
could not see it. A second `WP 7.1` puts two packages behind one name in the
single cell R8 reads to decide whether a defect has an owner at all. That is D104
happening again by a phase number instead of by a page title, so the phase is
**8**, and the routings dataset the original plan called Phase 8 is deferred in
§14 where additive work belongs.

**The gate moved with it, and it has teeth.** A phase inserted between §13 and §14
would renumber §15 and §16, which are cited by number from the sidecars, from
CLAUDE.md and from eleven hundred places inside this document — so Phase 8 is
§18, physically after §17. That put it outside the slice R7, R8 and R10 read.
`check.mjs` now builds its roadmap from **two ranges** (§7–§13 and §18) through
one `roadmapText()` helper, so a Phase 8 package is held to exactly what a Phase 3
package is. **Proved by the case rather than asserted beside it**: marking WP 8.0
✅ before writing this entry made R7 fail with the package named.

**── THE NUMBERS, AND THEY MOVED THE DIAGNOSIS TWICE ──**

Two §15 runs, both on this branch: `35433237514` (probes 1–7) and `35433474185`
(probes 8–10, written BECAUSE of what the first one said). Ten projects.

**The reported project's BOM is exactly four levels deep, so the defect the brief
predicted is LATENT there — and the map is still wrong, for a reason nothing in
the brief named.** `Project AA - ver3`: `bom_level = multi`, 396
`bom_multi_level` rows, `max(level) = 4`. On the brief's reading the ladder should
be correct. It is not, and probe 8 says why:

| | `bom_multi_level` | bom lane levels | inbound lane levels |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Project 2` | 396 rows, 4 deep | **1, 2, 3, 4** | 5 |
| `Project AA - ver3` | 396 rows, 4 deep | **2, and only 2** (397 rows) | **1, 5** |

Same BOM. Incompatible lanes. **There are two live ETLs** — that is D125, and it
is the finding of the package. `combine_project_into_supply_chain`, a SQL RPC
called from the policy grid, the data manager twice and the `projects` completion
trigger, writes `bom_multi_level` rows with a **literal `level = 2`** and never
reads `b.level`. The edge function writes `row.level || 1`. So AA-ver3's 4-deep
BOM renders FLAT — 260 materials and 66 products in one column, one colour, every
one labelled `material level 2` — and its suppliers split across level 1 (16 rows,
which the ladder calls a material) and level 5 (353 rows, which it calls a
supplier). **Two suppliers from one upload, four levels apart.** And WP 8.2 was
scoped to fix the edge function, which per D88 is not deployed: the live path is
the RPC, and a fix to the other half would have changed nothing and reported
success.

**D112 is live on AA-ver3 and on no other project.** 65 nodes are both a BOM
material and a BOM source — genuine **sub-assemblies**. `classify_node_type`
resolves all 65 to `product` by its priority order; the page resolves them to
`material level 2`. Sixty-five nodes, two confident answers, one screen apart.
AA-ver3 is also the only project with any untyped nodes: **29 `node_list` rows are
`unknown` or NULL**, and `ProductLevelNetwork` renders an unrecognised group as
**Supplier**.

**D127, which no code read predicted and which a user would call "the map looks
wrong" with no classifier involved.** AA-ver3's inbound lane holds **369 rows
against 321 in `inbound_logistics`** — 48 source rows left after the last combine
and nothing rebuilt the graph, because neither writer is a trigger on the lane's
sources. **And every freshness signal reports it fresh**: the lane was written
0.17 s AFTER `inbound_logistics` was last touched, because `max(updated_at)` does
not move when rows are DELETED. That is D12's lesson in a second place — a
timestamp asks whether a clock moved, and 48 rows leaving a table moves no clock.

**Two rows this package opened were OVER-CLAIMS, and §15 is what said so.**

- **D114 is latent.** Zero `bom_multi_level` rows have a blank
  `higher_level_component_id` in any project, and both edge tables hold zero empty
  endpoints — so there is no material→finished-product edge to drop. The sidecar
  says the column is *"empty at the top of the tree"* and production has never
  contained such a row, which is a finding about the contract as much as the data.
  The mechanism was also wrong: the row is lost in the **demand walk**, one stage
  before the `|| ''` a reader sees first, so a count of `''` could never have
  found it either way.
- **D126 is latent for the same reason** — 0 `ROOT` edges, 0 `ROOT` rows in
  `node_list` — and it was only found because the first report's zero empty
  endpoints looked too clean. The live RPC writes
  `COALESCE(higher_level_component_id, 'ROOT')` into both the edge endpoint and
  `path_root`: where the edge function drops the edge, this one **fabricates a
  node that no CSV contains**. T1 in one string, the same class as D124's "work
  station", arriving from SQL instead of TypeScript.

**D115 and D118 are live and exactly as predicted.** Three single-level projects
hold zero multi-tier rows (`Project 1`: 123 inbound rows, 0 lane rows — a
permanently empty Process page); `data_source_group` is written on **0 of 5 445**
rows. **D113 is live at scale**: **466 nodes** appear at more than one `level`, so
for 466 nodes the page's map is written by whichever row the loop read last.
**D117**: **104** multi-tier nodes have no `node_list` row at all.

**Verified:** `contract:check` ✓ (R6 resolves all 13 new citations in range, R7
append-only over 119 revisions, R8 44 packages named, R10 33 cross-checked) ·
`check:docs` ✓ · `contract:rehearse` ✓ (21 assertion files, unchanged — this
package adds no migration) · the seven probes `EXPLAIN` and then **execute**
against the rehearsal database built from the introspected schema, so a column
name that does not exist fails here rather than in the one workflow pointed at

**Gap check.** Four findings.

1. **The instrument was wrong about the question TWICE, and both times the report
   is what corrected it — not a re-read of the code.** Probes 1–7 were written from
   a careful reading and they measured the right columns for the wrong hypothesis:
   they established that AA-ver3's BOM is four levels deep, which on the brief's
   reading makes the ladder correct, and the map is still wrong. Probes 8–10 exist
   only because two projects with identical BOM tables disagreed about their own
   lane in the first report's output. **The lesson is the cost of a single
   measurement pass**: WP 8.1 should assume its own reading is a hypothesis, and the
   §15 door is cheap enough to use twice in one package.
2. **`InteractiveNetworkSpace` was outside `check:docs`'s data-layer list**, while
   the other three network pages were inside it. It is the fourth reader of the
   same table and the one WP 8.3 lifts its subgraph engine out of, so a citation of
   it in any document but this one was free to go stale. Added to `DATA_LAYER` in
   the same commit; the gate stays green because the one place outside §4 that
   cites it is already allow-listed for owning the mobile-layout subject.
3. **Seven probes do not measure the thing the user actually reported.** They
   measure `level`, identity, blanks and the projection. Nobody can currently
   measure "the map looks wrong", and WP 8.4's exit criterion — the same entity
   renders as the same node, in the same colour, with legend counts equal to node
   counts — is the first statement of it that a person can check in one pass. It is
   an *assertion by a reader*, not a gate, and this package does not pretend
   otherwise.
4. **D122 has an owner and no probe.** The function that returns products as
   materials joins the FIRM table, which per D19 holds rows in exactly one project
   — so its damage is bounded by a number §15 already measured, and adding an
   eighth probe would have re-measured it. Stated here so the omission is a
   decision rather than a gap.


### WP 8.1 — The classifier and the projection · 2026-09-19 · `20260919000001`

**What the previous package promised.** WP 8.0 closed with sixteen defects and one
recommendation: author node identity and node type ONCE, in `node_list`, because
the typed projection already exists and a new table would duplicate it. It also
handed over a number this package needed — 104 multi-tier nodes with no
`node_list` row (D117) — and a correction it had made to itself: two of its own
rows were over-claims, and §15 said so rather than a re-read.

**What this one shipped.** `node_list.echelon`, CHECK-constrained to seven values
including the `subassembly` no classifier in this repository could express;
`bom_depth` and `supply_tier` as **two** columns, because the single `level` they
replace conflates two measurements and that conflation IS the wrong mapping;
`classify_node_echelon` as the one rule, reading BOTH edge tables; and
`classify_node_type` kept — but as a **mapping** from that rule rather than a
second priority order beside it, so `MapView` and the legacy columns are unchanged
and the two cannot drift. That last part is `single-source` (I1) applied to a
function instead of to a document: there was never a way to compare the old
classifier's priority order with a page's, and now there is one order to compare
against.

**Every existing value that moves, moves in one direction and is named**: the 65
nodes §15 found that are both a BOM target and a BOM source were `product` and are
now `material` in `node_type` and `subassembly` in `echelon`. The old order tested
product before material, which told the map to draw a thing the plant consumes on
the customer side.

**── D128: THE TRIGGER HAS NEVER FIRED, IN THIRTEEN MONTHS ──**

`auto_refresh_node_list_on_scd_change` is attached `FOR EACH STATEMENT` to
`supply_chain_data` and its body is
`pid := COALESCE(NEW.project_id, OLD.project_id)`. **A statement-level trigger has
no `NEW` and no `OLD`.** PL/pgSQL leaves both unassigned, the field reference
yields NULL rather than raising, the guard is false, and the function returns
having done nothing — since 2025-08-29.

Demonstrated rather than reasoned about, on a real PostgreSQL 16:

```
NOTICE:  pid=<NULL>
```

This is D80's shape — a whole mechanism whose failure has no symptom — in the one
place it silently degrades data a user looks at, because **a refresh that does not
happen looks exactly like a graph that has not changed.** It is also the other half
of D117's answer: `node_list` has been refreshed ONLY by the `projects.completed`
row-level trigger and by a one-off backfill loop from 2025-08-31, which is why §15
found 242 `node_list` rows against 294 graph nodes on the project a user reported.

Fixed with a **transition table** — `REFERENCING NEW TABLE`, which is what a
statement-level trigger has instead of `NEW`, available since PostgreSQL 10 — on
BOTH edge tables, statement level and deliberately not per row (§4 D76 is what
row-level costs here: 2 129 recomputations of one graph). The old function is left
in place with a comment saying it is dead, rather than dropped, so a later
`CREATE OR REPLACE` cannot quietly resurrect it into a trigger.

**── AND FIXING IT TURNED TWO REHEARSALS RED, WHICH IS THE REAL FINDING ──**

`rehearsal/090` and `/110` failed with `forbidden`, raised from
`rebuild_node_list` line 19, reached through the newly-alive trigger inside an
ordinary `INSERT INTO supply_chain_data`.

`rebuild_node_list` AUTHORIZES: it refuses unless the current user is the project's
modeler or an admin in the same organization. That was harmless while the refresh
ran only from the completion trigger and from explicit client calls. The moment a
LANE trigger fires for real, the derivation runs inside somebody else's statement —
and re-deciding an authorization there can only ever refuse a writer the database
has already allowed.

**A derivation is not a decision.** That is §4 D66 exactly, and
`20260917000005` is the precedent this package followed rather than rediscovered:
a role gate was written into the shared writer preamble, found to refuse an
organization admin on `combine-project`'s live path, and removed, because
`min_project_role` is D66's to make live and not each writer's to answer ad hoc.

So discovery was split from authorization. `node_list_discover` does the node-set
insert, names its actor through `assert_writer_may_act` — the same shared preamble,
which refuses a NULL actor and sets `app.current_user_id` LOCAL — and decides
nothing. `rebuild_node_list` keeps its check for the clients that call it directly
and delegates the insert. **`dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` is what put the attribution
line there**: the first draft wrote a tier-3 table with no GUC and the ratchet
failed with the new function named, which is the gate behaving exactly as
CLAUDE.md's `audit-actor` row describes.

**── WHAT THIS PACKAGE DID NOT DO, STATED SO IT IS A DECISION ──**

1. **Identity is still `(project_id, node_id)`.** D116 wanted compound identity so
   a firm that is both a supplier and a customer stays two roles on one entity.
   §15 measured **0** such firms in production, so a migration was not spent on it;
   the row says latent rather than closed, and WP 8.3 owns the page-side half.
2. **`supply_tier` reaches 2 and 3 only for a firm that also appears in an edge
   table.** `node_list` is the projection of the two edge tables, and a firm that
   exists only in `tier2_suppliers` is not a node of that graph — folding the
   deep-tier FIRM graph in is a different node universe (`network_nodes.uid`
   against material ids is D122). **Asserted rather than assumed**: `rehearsal/230`
   §4 fails if such a firm acquires a `node_list` row, so a later package that
   widens the projection has to change that line deliberately.
3. **Nothing touched `supply_chain_data_multi_tier.level`.** Two live writers
   disagree about what it means (D125) and choosing between them is WP 8.2's first
   act, not a side effect of this file.
4. **No column joined `graph_hash`.** `node_list` is wholly outside it and these
   three columns are derived; folding them in would put an output inside the
   identity of its own inputs, which is what `input-hash` (I5) exists to prevent.

including `--since HEAD` against the artifact this branch writes, which is the mode
D52 exists for · 534 tests ✓ · `typecheck` ✓ 28 of 28 held · `check:docs` ✓ ·
`contract:generate` committed.

**`supabase/rehearsal/230`, five sections, mutation-tested five ways:**

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| remove the `is_bom_source AND is_bom_target` branch | §2 red — a subassembly reports `product` |
| discovery reads `supply_chain_data` only again | §3 red — the deep-tier-only node has no row |
| `supply_tier` returns `COALESCE(…, 0)` instead of NULL | §4 red — D119's substitution, caught in a new column |
| re-attach the old `NEW`-reading trigger | **the MIGRATION fails** — and that is how a real defect in it was found |
| the refresh calls the checked `rebuild_node_list` again | `090` and `110` red with `forbidden`, **not** 230 |

**Gap check.** Four findings.

1. **A mutation found a defect in the migration that no assertion did.** The three
   `supply_chain_data` triggers had no `DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS`, so the file could
   not be applied twice — `contract:rehearse` reports it as a RUN-TIME failure a
   static replay cannot see (§4 D31). The scdmt half had its DROPs all along, which
   is what made the asymmetry look deliberate. **Mutation-testing the rehearsal
   tested the migration**, which is not what it was for.
2. **The two mutations that matter most are caught by OTHER files.** `090` and
   `110` are what fail when the refresh re-authorizes, not `230` — because 230's
   actor IS the project's modeler, so the check it would hit passes. The rehearsal
   header says so explicitly rather than claiming coverage it does not have, and
   the general lesson is that a package's own rehearsal is not the whole of its
   safety net.
3. **`echelon` is authored once and read by nothing.** Eight classifiers still run
   at render time; this package removed none of them, because deleting a page's
   classifier before the column it would read is populated in production is a
   change that cannot be verified. WP 8.3 owns the readers, and `oneClassifier.test.ts`
   is what makes "eight became one" a gate rather than a claim — **until it exists,
   the eight can still become nine.**
4. **The backfill is in the migration, and that is the one irreversible thing
   here.** WP 4.3 shipped `computed_from_hash` nullable and D88 is what that cost:
   8 577 rows that predate provenance and a drop nobody can take. So `echelon` is
   filled for every existing row in the migration that adds it — but the same
   statement re-derives `node_type`, which MOVES the 65 subassemblies. That is the
   only stored value this package changes, it is named in D112's row and in the
   migration's section 8, and it is reversible only by re-running the old
   classifier, which no longer exists.


### WP 8.3 (partial) — The shared graph layer · 2026-09-19 · `20260919000002`

**What the previous package promised.** WP 8.1 closed with a countable handover:
`echelon` authored once, and "the eight render-time classifiers all still run, so
the fact is authored once and believed eight times". WP 8.3 was to move the
readers.

**It also promised "no migration", and that was wrong for a reason nobody could
have read off the sidecar.** See D130 below.

**── WHAT THIS PACKAGE ORDERED DIFFERENTLY, AND WHY ──**

§18 puts WP 8.2 (one ETL) before WP 8.3, on the premise that the pages need a
corrected `level`. **After WP 8.1 they do not.** A page reading `echelon` and
`bom_depth` from `node_list` is independent of
`supply_chain_data_multi_tier.level` entirely — and `bom_depth` comes from
`bom_multi_level`, which the flattening D125 describes never touched. So the
shared layer **fixes the reported map without the ETL being changed at all**, and
doing it first means WP 8.2 can then change `level` freely because nothing reads
it. WP 8.2 is also the one package in this phase that alters stored production
data, which is a reason to take it with the readers already off that column
rather than before.

**── WHAT LANDED ──**

`src/lib/graph/`, 85 tests. The vocabulary (seven values, compound
`{ echelon, id }` identity); **one** palette where there were five; the encodings;
the extracted subgraph engine and focus walk; and the read path.

**Three encoding claims are now tested rather than asserted.** Size scales by
`sqrt`, so AREA and not diameter carries the value — a diameter-linear scale makes
a 4× value look 16×, and the test asserts the correction rather than the
convenience. Edge width is log-scaled, because supply flows span orders of
magnitude and a linear scale renders everything but the largest as the hairline
that made a flat 1.5 look acceptable. A **zero-flow arc still draws**, at minimum
width, because a zero-weighted arc is a real finding (D2/D3) and hiding it is the
opposite of disclosing it. And a **null metric is not drawn small** — small means
a low value, null means no value, so it renders uniform and the page marks it.

**`subgraphParity.test.ts` is what makes the extraction a fact rather than a
hope.** `InteractiveNetworkSpace` is in no menu and reachable only by URL, so
nobody would notice if the extraction changed its behaviour. The original is
reproduced VERBATIM as a frozen witness and 21 query cases run through both. It is
the one place in this repository where a duplicate is right: the copy is not a
source a reader might follow, it is a recording of the behaviour being preserved.
It also carries an anti-vacuity check, because a parity suite where both sides
return nothing for every case passes and proves nothing.

**── TWO DEFECTS FOUND BY EXTRACTING, NOT BY READING ──**

**D129 — `includeTerminals` is inverted.** The walk stops at a `stopUp`/`stopDown`
level only `if (includeTerminals)`, and the default is `false`. So the parameter
does the opposite of what its name says and the whole terminal-stop mechanism has
**never bounded a single walk under its own default**. Reproduced faithfully
rather than fixed — parity is the extraction's guarantee, and a refactor that also
changes behaviour can be verified as neither. `respectTerminals` is the opt-in
fix, and the parity suite asserts BOTH readings so the defect cannot be quietly
un-reproduced.

**D130 — a fixed `RETURNS TABLE` is a second place the schema is authored.**
`get_node_list` is the only route to `node_list` from the application, and it lists
seventeen columns BY NAME. WP 8.1 added three; `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` cannot
change a return type; **nothing failed, and a type that was authored, backfilled
and CHECK-constrained was invisible to every page in the product.** That is
`single-source` (I1) broken in SQL rather than in markdown — the same blind spot
D101 and D105 came out of — and `contract:validate` cannot see it, because the
sidecar describes the TABLE and no rule compares a table's columns against the
projections claiming to return them.

Closed for this table by an **additive** `get_graph_nodes` rather than by widening
`get_node_list`: that would be a DROP and CREATE, `get_node_list` has four live
callers, and `20260918000003` is the record of what a DROP costs — it takes the
function's grants with it, which `rehearsal/210` §2 had to verify by checking every
role back as an explicit `proacl` grantee because `has_function_privilege` cannot
fail while PUBLIC keeps EXECUTE. **The CLASS is open and owned**: no gate counts
the schema's other fixed `RETURNS TABLE`s against the tables they project.

`get_graph_nodes` deliberately does NOT return the criticality prediction. That is
analysis output, it belongs to a run, and a page that wants it should ask the
analysis store rather than read it off an entity row (D19).

**── WHAT DID NOT LAND, AS A NUMBER ──**

**All six `src/` classifiers are still in place, and both gates are RATCHETS
because of it.** Deleting a page's classifier before `echelon` is populated for
every project in production is a change nobody can verify, and D88 is what
shipping the unverifiable half looks like. So the baselines ARE the handover:

| | count |
|---|---|
| classifiers in `src/` | **6** — `buildGroupClassification` + `getLocationGroup`, `getNodeTypeFromLevel` + `getDisplayNodeType`, `getTierFromDepth`, `getNodeTypeFromLevel` |
| colour literals, Product / Process / Firm / Interactive / Map | **11 / 32 / 13 / 16 / 18** |

Both ratchets fail if a number RISES **and** if it falls without the baseline
falling with it, so neither can go stale the way an assertion of zero would. One
line of gate per classifier gone is what makes the remaining work countable
instead of described (D90's lesson).

**Verified:** `contract:check` ✓ · `contract:rehearse` ✓ all three ways ·
**619 tests ✓ (was 534)** · `typecheck` ✓ 28 of 28 held, over 478 files where it
was 466 · `check:docs` ✓ · **`eslint` unchanged at 452 problems**, so the module
added none — the RPC shim is a narrow structural cast rather than the `any` the
nine existing call sites use · `rehearsal/230` §6 mutation-tested two ways (drop
`echelon` from the projection → red; reverse the ordering `CASE` → red).

**── WP 8.5's LABELS RODE ALONG, AND R12 CAUGHT THE COST ──**

`getDisplayNodeType` no longer returns **"work station"** — a noun no table in
`supabase/contract/` can produce, invented from `level === 1`, and the plainest
**T1** breach in this area. It also stopped returning `material level N`: that
column is not a depth (D125), and on the measured project the string called 260
materials and 66 products "material level 2" at once. The title, the empty state
and the legend heading now say what the data is.

**And shifting those lines turned `contract:check` R12 red on four sidecar lineage
citations** — `bom_multi_level`, `supply_chain_data_multi_tier` (twice) and
`projects` all cite a `file:line` in that page, and a comment inserted above them
moved every one. That is D21 and D22's exact mechanism, caught the same minute
rather than a quarter later, which is what R12 was built for. Re-pointed in the same
commit.

**Gap check.** Five findings.

1. **The layer is built and read by nothing.** That is the honest state and the
   ratchets say so in numbers rather than in prose. It is also the risk: a module
   with 85 tests and no caller is a module that can drift from what the pages
   actually need, and the only cure is migrating one page soon enough to find out.
2. **D130 is a rule this repository does not have.** `contract:check` compares
   sidecars against tables and PLAN citations against files; nothing compares a
   function's declared projection against the table it projects. The instance is
   closed and the class is one `pg_proc` query away — it is named in §4 rather
   than written here because a gate added in the same breath as its first instance
   is a gate tested against exactly one case.
3. **The parity witness will go stale by design.** It records
   `InteractiveNetworkSpace` as of today. When WP 8.4 migrates that page to the
   extracted engine the witness becomes a recording of something no longer in the
   tree — which is correct (it is a frozen measurement, not a mirror) but the test
   file must say so at that point or a reader will try to keep them in step.
4. **The focus walk cannot chain through one echelon.** Each step must ADVANCE
   along the chain, so three nested sub-assemblies stop the walk after the first.
   The test asserts that limit explicitly rather than hiding it; fixing it needs
   `bom_depth` as a tie-break within a band, which is WP 8.4's when a page offers
   a depth-aware focus.
5. **A label change cost four lineage citations, and that is a cost worth
   naming.** Every `file:line` in a sidecar's `surfaces` is a fact about a line
   number, so any edit above it is a documentation change too. R12 makes that
   visible in seconds rather than in a quarter — but the underlying brittleness is
   real, and the only durable fix is anchoring lineage on a TOKEN rather than on a
   line, which is what §4's own R6 already does ("anchored elsewhere"). Not
   attempted here; named so the next package that edits a page with lineage entries
   is not surprised.
